Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

charge noun and verb

an accusation

also accusation, accuse, charge with, be charged with, bring charges, indict, indictment, allege, allegation, false allegation, false charge, capital charge, accuse of a capital offence, bring charges against, file charges, count (of an indictment), charge with a crime, accuse of a capital crime, false accusation, charge someone with a crime

classical

Phaedr. 1.10.4: lupus arguēbat vulpem fūrtī crīmine
Traupman 194
Traupman 194: count
Traupman 289
Traupman 297

crīmen, crīminis n.

noun, third declension

charge, accusation

To bring charges against someone: crīmina alicuī īnferre (Traupman 194).

Other words

  • arguō, arguere, arguī, argūtum — charge (someone with), accuse

    verb, third conjugation, with the accusative of the person and the genitive or ablative of the charge · also used · classical · Phaedr. 1.10.4: fūrtī crīmine; Traupman 194; Traupman 193: allege

    aliquem crīmine (or dē crīmine, crīminis) arguere (Traupman 194).

  • accūsō, accūsāre, accūsāvī, accūsātum — accuse; blame

    verb, first conjugation, with the accusative of the person and the genitive or dē of the charge · also used · classical · Traupman 193; Publil. Sent. N 25: Nēminem citō accūsāverīs

    Of a formal accusation, and of finding fault in general.

  • reum facere — bring a charge against, prosecute

    phrase: reus, reī m. (the accused) with facere and the accusative of the person · also used · classical · Nep. Alc. 4.3 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 193, 195: indict

  • accūsātiō, accūsātiōnis f. — an accusation, an indictment

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 2.14: ratiō jūdiciōrum ex accūsātiōne et dēfēnsiōne cōnstat (Lewis & Short); Traupman 193; Cic. (Lewis & Short); Traupman 268

  • calumnia, calumniae f. — a false charge; chicanery

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Lewis & Short s.v. calumnia: trickery, chicanery; in law, false accusation; Traupman 194; Lewis & Short: “trickery, chicanery”; in law, a false accusation; Traupman 289

  • īnsimulātiō, īnsimulātiōnis f. — an allegation, a charge

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Font. 13.29: in falsam atque inīquam probrōrum īnsimulātiōnem vocābātur (Lewis & Short); Traupman 270

Examples

  • lupus arguēbat vulpem fūrtī crīmine; negābat illa sē esse culpae proximam

    the wolf charged the fox with theft; she denied that she was anywhere near guiltyPhaedr. 1.10.4–5

  • Difficilem habēre oportet aurem ad crīmina.

    one should have an ear that is slow to listen to accusationsPublil. Sent. D 11

  • aliquem reī capitālis reum facere

    to accuse someone of a capital offenceTraupman 193

  • crīmina alicui īnferre

    to bring charges against someoneTraupman 190, 194

  • aliquem crīmine (dē crīmine) arguere

    to charge someone with a crimeTraupman 194

  • capitāle crīmen

    a capital chargeTraupman 194

  • falsa īnsimulātiō

    a false allegationTraupman 193; cf. Cic. Font. 29: in falsam atque inīquam probrōrum īnsimulātiōnem (Lewis & Short s.v. īnsimulātiō)

  • Hortēnsius eum pecūlātūs accūsāvit.

    Hortensius accused him of embezzlement.Traupman 190

  • aliquem reum capitālis reī facere

    to accuse someone of a capital offenceTraupman 268

  • aliquem crīmine (dē crīmine, crīminis) arguere

    to charge someone with a crimeTraupman 289

See also accept blame, police officer.
